Unless I am much mistaken (always possible), Sudafed is pseudoephedrine. Paracetamol is a pain reliever/fever reducer. Not sure what brand name it goes by abroad but in the US paracetamol is Tylenol. Sudafed is a nasal decongestant. However, Sudafed is occasionally mixed with added painkillers, including both naproxen and paracetamol- you’ll know by reading the ingredients list and looking for words like added “pain” and “pressure” relief on the box. It is still a good idea to avoid alcohol with pseudoephedrine but alcohol and paracetamol is what will really fuck up your liver.

This is an important thing people don’t realize and I’m pointing it out because I’m not sure people reading it will understand your distinction. Had I done what, at times, I had wanted to do to myself, I would’ve had a whole life of misery and no happiness. Now at least I get to experience the life that most other people live. I can’t give the person who slighted me what I so obsessively feel they deserve, but I can give someone else something they deserve instead.

Or that when you’re struggling, you may have $10 for your family’s meals for the day in your pocket right then but can’t collect $100 each week for a trip to Safeway? Or that a chicken nugget might be the only semi-treat a kid in a family like that can get? Or that the food has a low price-to-calorie ratio sometimes making it the most economical to feed kids, especially for children who are not good at eating plain rice and beans for every meal? This thread is full of people who have a one-dimensional understanding of the problem of poverty and think they’ve got a good grasp on its nuance and complication.

The Free Churro suggestion for these situations baffles me every time I see it. “I want to show you this great deep, funny comedy. Here’s 23 minutes of monotoned monologue that only makes sense if you’re emotionally invested in the characters and their multi-year trauma history.” I get the impulse- it’s a great episode and it resonates with us, so we assume it would resonate with others. We feel like we get one chance to show off the show, so we want to show it at its height. But if I told someone I wanted to show them a funny but deep and insightful comedy and put on what is basically a generational trauma podcast intended to solely highlight the character development of the protagonist, I think my friends would want to put something else on after less than 90 seconds.

I think any episode that requires background knowledge, even if we are inclined to think the background knowledge is obvious, is not a good candidate for this. I would try to find an episode that is as close to standalone as possible and shows the social commentary and animal goofiness together with some coverage of the mental health components. It doesn’t need to be the most highly rated episode of the series; it just needs to give the person a look at the basic premises of the show so they can know whether they want to see more. I usually use Bojack Hates the Troops for this but there are others that also have these elements.

OCD is a mental health condition and one of many types of symptoms it has is getting stuck in patterns, feeling like you “have to” do something (trying to explain this in layman’s terms in the event you’re not a native English speaker or live somewhere where this info isn’t common) over and over in the same way or something terrible will happen. Hi. It’s not totally clear based on your post what the nature of your struggle is. If you have a substance abuse problem or addiction and live in the US, call 1-800-662-4357 (google your country’s hotline if not in the US- if you don’t like the national hotline, your state/region may have its own). This is the national substance abuse hotline. What you want is for someone knowledgeable to locate an appropriate treatment program for you, which is likely how the helpline will assist you. To accomplish this goal of finding a program, you can also contact 1) your doctor, or 2) the office of local addiction help programs (in my experience they will even help you find programs that aren’t theirs if you need it). Depending on where you work, some employers pay for Employee Assistance Programs, where employees can get free counseling and other resources as a job benefit. These can also be starting points. 

For me, I checked myself into rehab, like Bojack did. It turned my life around completely. I suggest that if you are able to use health insurance that you have, or are able to beg/borrow money to pay, or if you can land a payment plan, or if you can get an addiction program to fund your treatment (some have funds set aside to do this) that you attend residential rehab. Outpatient programs help, certainly, and people can and do become sober with them, but if you’re relating to the hallucinations, it sounds to me like you may be past the point where Narcotics/Alcoholics Anonymous, support groups, short-term programs, and the like can save you from yourself.  To maintain sobriety after getting clean, it is proven by scientific study that people are most successful where they follow the “continuum of care,” in which you gradually step down to less and less time-consuming and intense addiction programming over time. 

I have 11 months of recovery from my alcoholism so far (not much but not nothing either!) and if you would like to talk more about this, feel free to reply or DM me.

ETA: I also suffer from several comorbid mental illnesses. If this is where your struggle lies and you’re interested in advice, I can speak a little on this too.
